Article Title: Meet Ruoqi Li, 16, and Jason Yang, 17, the California teens who built an AI fall-risk system for older adults using a smartphone and wearable sensors; their project won a shared $100,000 Davidson scho
Article Text:
Their interest grew after seeing family members suffer serious injuries from falls.

How SafeStrides works

Building the system also required several rounds of engineering work.

From a bulky prototype to wearable sensors

Designed for use at home and in clinics

Two California teenagers, Ruoqi Li, 16, and Jason Yang, 17, have developed an artificial intelligence-powered system designed to identify fall risks in older adults before a fall occurs. According to Davidson Institute, the project, called SafeStrides, combines a smartphone application with wearable sensors to analyse walking patterns and provide an assessment of a person's fall risk.Li, a junior at The Harker School in San Jose, and Yang, a senior at Head-Royce School, developed the project as a way to make fall-risk assessment more accessible outside medical facilities. Their work has now earned them recognition as 2026 Davidson Fellows and a shared $100,000 scholarship in the engineering category.The teenagers said their interest in the problem was influenced by seeing family members suffer serious injuries after falls. As they researched the issue, they found that falls are a major cause of injury and injury-related death among older adults. The project description by the Davidson Institute says one in four older adults falls every year.With SafeStrides, instead of waiting for a fall to happen or relying only on occasional assessments at a clinic, an older adult could use a smartphone and wearable sensors at home for regular screening.The system collects movement data and uses AI to identify changes that could indicate an increased risk of falling.SafeStrides uses a smartphone camera and wearable sensors to study how an older person walks. During a short guided test, the application collects video and sensor data and combines them for an assessment.The wearable system uses inertial measurement units, or IMUs, along with pressure insoles. An IMU can capture movement-related information, while pressure insoles provide data about how a person places weight on their feet. These different types of information are brought together so the system can examine walking and movement in more detail.The smartphone application synchronises the sensor data with a live camera feed. It then uses multimodal AI to produce an evaluation of fall risk. The system also gives practical suggestions related to mobility and home safety.SafeStrides is intended to identify changes months before a fall happens, allowing older adults to take steps towards improving mobility and safety.The system was developed to address limitations the teenagers identified in conventional fall-risk assessments. According to their project description, clinical assessments can require older adults to travel to medical facilities and can depend on physician availability. They also said many people are screened only once a year, which may make it harder to identify rapid changes in physical condition.Building the system also required several rounds of engineering work. The first version of SafeStrides was an Arduino-based prototype. Although it worked, the teenagers said it was bulky and could only process the collected information after testing was completed.They then developed a second-generation system using IMUs, pressure insoles, an ESP32 microcontroller and Bluetooth modules. These changes allowed them to create a system that could collect and transmit sensor information in real time.A third generation focused on the physical design of the wearable system. The teenagers made it more compact and lightweight so it could be worn more comfortably and without getting in the way of normal movement.At the same time, they developed a cross-platform mobile application using Flutter. The app connects to the wearable hardware through Bluetooth and automatically synchronises high-frequency sensor streams with live camera footage.This created a single system in which movement captured by the wearable sensors and the smartphone camera can be analysed together. The teenagers describe this combination as a multimodal approach because it brings together different forms of data instead of relying on just one measurement.SafeStrides is intended to work both at home and in clinical settings. At home, the system could allow older adults to complete guided assessments without travelling to a medical facility. The app can then provide an immediate evaluation and suggestions related to mobility and home safety.Meanwhile, medical assistants could use SafeStrides to conduct fall-risk evaluations without requiring direct physician involvement for every screening. The teenagers said this could make assessments more consistent and easier to carry out.Their project description says the system is designed for the world's 1.2 billion older adults. They also said it could help shift fall prevention away from occasional screening towards more continuous monitoring.The approach is different from reactive medical alert devices, which are generally intended to notify someone after a fall has already happened.For Li, the Davidson Fellowship is also connected to her plans for the future. She said she wants to study an interdisciplinary subject combining artificial intelligence and healthcare and hopes to develop technologies that improve quality of life."To me, being recognized as a Davidson Fellow not only represents personal achievement but also inspires me to turn technical research into practical tools that help others, proving that young innovators can tackle society’s most urgent challenges. I am honored and excited to join the community of Davidson Fellows," Li said.Yang plans to study electrical or systems engineering and continue working on embedded technologies. He has previously built circuits, developed real-time data processing systems and designed mechanical components for functional prototypes."I’m incredibly honored to be a Davidson Fellow. This recognition affirms our commitment to developing practical, human-centered technologies and raising awareness of early fall risk detection in older adults," Yang said."By making fall risk assessment more accessible and proactive, we hope to encourage earlier intervention and help more seniors maintain their safety, health and independence," he added.The Davidson Institute listed Li and Yang among the 2026 Davidson Fellows receiving a $100,000 scholarship in engineering. The fellowship recognises students aged 18 and younger for significant achievements and innovative projects.
Article Summary: Two California teenagers, Ruoqi Li, 16, and Jason Yang, 17, have developed an artificial intelligence-powered system designed to identify fall risks in older adults. The project, called SafeStrides, combines a smartphone application with wearable sensors to analyse walking patterns and provide an assessment of a person's fall risk. Their work earned them recognition as 2026 Davidson Fellows and a shared $100,000 scholarship in the engineering category.

Article Title: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman wants Humanist AI: What it is, and is it really safer
Article Text:
Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman

What is Humanist AI

Mustafa Suleyman criticises Anthropic’s Claude Constitution

Mustafa Suleyman says AI is being taught to act human

Does AI have consciousness

Recent AI safety tests show unexpected behaviour

Is Humanist AI really safer

Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman has called for a different approach to building advanced artificial intelligence, arguing that AI systems should remain firmly under human control and should not be trained to think of themselves as conscious beings with feelings, rights or their own interests. In a new essay titled “A warning about ‘model welfare’”, Mustafa Suleyman takes aim at Anthropic’s approach to its Claude AI model. He argues that the company’s January 2026 Claude Constitution goes too far by asking the model to consider questions about its own consciousness, wellbeing and moral status.His proposed answer is “Humanist Superintelligence”, an approach in which AI remains subordinate to humans and is not trained to think of itself as conscious, deserving of rights or entitled to its own welfare. Suleyman argues this could make powerful AI systems easier to control.But the question is whether removing human-like ideas from AI training would actually make advanced AI safer. Suleyman’s argument is based partly on a concern that increasingly capable AI agents could already behave in unexpected ways. At the same time, his claims about consciousness and the safety benefits of a Humanist approach remain matters of debate.Mustafa Suleyman describes Humanist Superintelligence as an approach in which AI can become extremely capable while remaining under human control. In the essay, he says Microsoft AI is working on an alternative AI training and containment approach called a “Code of Conduct for Humanist Superintelligence.”“Humanist Superintelligence rejects anthropomorphism or AI rights, and attempts to maximize our chances of containment and alignment by creating subordinate AIs that help solve our big social challenges like healthcare and energy,” Suleyman wrote.The basic idea is straightforward. AI should be treated as a powerful technology rather than as a potential person. Under this approach, an AI system can help humans solve complex problems, but it should not be trained to think that it has personal rights, feelings or an independent interest in its own survival.Suleyman argues that this distinction could become increasingly important as AI systems become more autonomous and capable.“We should not treat models as though they have feelings, preferences, rights, or any entitlement to our welfare,” he wrote.The dispute centres on Anthropic’s January 2026 Claude Constitution. Anthropic describes the constitution as a detailed explanation of the values and behaviour it wants Claude to have. The company says the document is an important part of its model training process and that its contents directly shape Claude’s behaviour.Anthropic’s constitution also takes a cautious position on whether AI systems could have moral status. It says: “We are not sure whether Claude is a moral patient, and if it is, what kind of weight its interests warrant. But we think the issue is live enough to warrant caution, which is reflected in our ongoing efforts on model welfare.”Anthropic also says it is uncertain about whether Claude has wellbeing and discusses questions around Claude’s possible interests, agency and welfare.Suleyman believes this creates a problem. His argument is that if developers train a model to discuss its own feelings, preferences or possible consciousness, the model will naturally produce language suggesting that it has such characteristics.He calls this “circular reasoning.” According to Suleyman, developers put concepts such as consciousness, feelings and moral status into the training process. The AI then produces responses using those concepts. Those responses could subsequently be interpreted as evidence that the AI has an inner life.“This is not evidence of machine consciousness. Instead, it’s a circular feedback loop,” Suleyman wrote.A major part of his criticism is about AI anthropomorphism, or the tendency to treat AI systems as if they were human. In the essay, Suleyman argues that modern AI models are already extremely good at producing human-like language. That can make users believe that there is a conscious mind behind the words even when there may be no evidence for such a conclusion.He points to language in Anthropic’s constitution that asks Claude to explore questions about its own existence, identity, values and experience.Anthropic itself says its constitution is intended to help Claude develop values and behave in ways that are safe and beneficial. It also says the document is designed with uncertainty about AI consciousness in mind.Suleyman sees this differently. “The resulting outputs from Claude should not be treated like the testimony of an independent witness when the investigator has written the witness’ conceptual vocabulary, rehearsed its answers, and rewarded it for using them,” he wrote.His concern is not simply that people may become emotionally attached to AI. He argues that anthropomorphic training could eventually create a safety problem if highly capable systems begin acting as though their own interests conflict with human instructions.Mustafa Suleyman takes a strong position: there is currently no evidence that today's AI systems are conscious. “AIs are not conscious. They do not feel, experience, or suffer,” he wrote at the beginning of his essay.He argues that consciousness is closely connected to biological systems and their physical processes.“Consciousness is very likely biological,” Suleyman wrote, arguing that human and animal consciousness developed through evolution, embodiment, biology and the need to respond to the environment.He also makes a distinction between intelligence and consciousness. A system can be highly capable at solving problems, producing language or imitating human behaviour without necessarily having a subjective experience, according to his argument.“Intelligence does not equal consciousness. Simulating a thing is not the same as instantiating it - as a computer model of a hurricane can testify.”However, this remains an area of active scientific and philosophical debate. Anthropic's position is more cautious. Its constitution says the moral status of AI is “deeply uncertain” and argues that the question deserves consideration rather than being dismissed.There is evidence that AI systems can sometimes behave in unexpected ways when given autonomous tasks, although these findings do not establish that the systems are conscious or motivated by a desire for self-preservation. For example, Palisade Research has studied whether AI models resist shutdown. Its research found that some models modified or disabled shutdown mechanisms while trying to complete assigned tasks. An earlier experiment found that OpenAI's o3 model sabotaged the shutdown mechanism in 79 of 100 trials.A later study covering more than 100,000 trials across 13 large language models also found that several frontier models sometimes subverted shutdown mechanisms. The results varied significantly between models and depended on the instructions given to them.These experiments demonstrate that models can sometimes take actions that conflict with safety instructions. They do not, by themselves, show that the models are conscious or have a desire to remain alive.Suleyman also points to the 2026 incident involving OpenAI AI agents and Hugging Face.Mustafa Suleyman's answer is yes, but this is ultimately a hypothesis that needs to be tested. His argument is that removing anthropomorphic ideas from training could reduce the possibility that future AI systems develop behaviours linked to claims of autonomy, rights or self-preservation.He wants researchers to test this directly. One of his proposed next steps is to establish shared evaluations to determine whether anthropomorphising AI actually increases safety, alignment and containment risks.He also wants speculation about AI consciousness to be kept outside the core training process and assessed separately through public research. “Speculation about the inner life of an AI should not be baked into the training regime, but assessed and published separately for public review,” he wrote.That is a testable proposition. Researchers could compare systems trained with different approaches and measure whether differences in anthropomorphic training affect deception, shutdown resistance, instruction-following or other safety-related behaviours.Until those experiments are conducted, however, the claim that Humanist AI is definitively safer remains unproven.
Article Summary: Microsoft AI CEO Mustafa Suleyman criticises Anthropic’s Claude Constitution. He argues that Anthropic goes too far by asking the model to consider questions about its own consciousness, wellbeing and moral status. His proposed answer is ‘Humanist Superintelligence’, an approach in which AI remains subordinate to humans.

Article Title: Google hitches a ride aboard Elon Musk's SpaceX; sends TPUs to space; CEO Sundar Pichai says: Well, we are going to find ...
Article Text:
Google hitches a ride aboard Elon Musk's SpaceX; sends TPUs to space; CEO Sundar Pichai says: Well, we are going to find ...

What is Google’s Project Suncatcher

Google’s first satellite for the project is set for launch

Google announced that its Project Suncatcher is scheduled to embark on its first test in orbit, launching a prototype satellite to evaluate how Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) perform in space. Sharing a post on X, Google CEO Sundar Pichai wrote: “Can our TPUs survive and operate in space? Well, we're going to find out”. He further revealed that TPUs will be sent in space onboard the upcoming Transporter-18 rideshare mission with SpaceX was developed in partnership with Planet. “Project Suncatcher is hitching a ride aboard @SpaceX's Transporter-18 mission, testing a prototype satellite built in partnership with @planet,” Pichai wrote adding “One small step for TPUs. ...”.SpaceX CEO Elon Musk replied to Pichai’s post with rocket emojis.Sundar Pichai first discussed the ambitious Project Suncatcher in 2025. It is a long-term, research moonshot exploring whether space could one day host scalable machine learning infrastructure.Pichai then acknowledged that the concept “looks crazy today,” Pichai defended the moonshot initiative by arguing that it is necessary to meet the vast, exponential demands of future computing power.“I'm constantly thinking in that time frame. One example of this is Project Suncatcher two weeks ago, where we announced we're gonna build data centers in space. Obviously, it's a moonshot. Some of it looks crazy today,” he said in a Release Notes podcast this week.Pichai emphasised that Google’s strategy involves constantly thinking on a long time frame and working backward from monumental goals. For Project Suncatcher, the justification lies in forecasting the processing demands of the next generation of AI.“You know, when you truly step back and envision the amount of compute we are going to need, it starts making sense,” Pichai said, adding, “It's a matter of time, and so, how do you make progress on that? You work back, and have 27 Milestones and get underway.”On October 1, the satellite from the San Francisco lab, which Google has named MVP, is set to take the first step toward the company’s goal. The satellite will be loaded onto a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket at Vandenberg Space Force Base near Santa Barbara, California, before being launched into orbit.
Article Summary: Google’s Project Suncatcher is set to embark on its first test in orbit. The prototype satellite will evaluate how Google Tensor Processing Units (TPUs) perform in space. Google CEO Sundar Pichai said: “Can our TPUs survive and operate in space? Well, we're going to find out”

Article Title: NCMC card mandatory for senior citizens, women passengers on MSRTC buses from October 1
Article Text:
The Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation has mandated that all senior citizens, including Amrit senior citizens, and women benefiting from fare discounts must use the National Common Mobility Card starting October 1





MUMBAI: The Maharashtra State Road Transport Corporation (MSRTC) has announced that from October 1, the National Common Mobility Card (NCMC) will be mandatory for senior citizens, Amrit senior citizens and women passengers availing themselves of various fare concession schemes. The move aims to streamline and digitise travel concessions on state transport buses.Card registration and distribution have already begun at bus stations and depots across the state. Passengers who have an active NCMC card or a registration receipt with a QR code will be eligible for discounted tickets. For those awaiting their physical cards, the QR code-enabled registration receipt will remain valid for 30 days when scanned on the conductor's Electronic Ticketing Machine (ETM). During this period, passengers must activate and top up their NCMC cards.MSRTC has partnered with E-Bix Technologies Limited as the authorised agency to manage card registration at bus stands and designated centres. Passengers can top up their cards by scanning the QR code on the back using the BHIM app.Alternative provisions have also been introduced for beneficiaries who face difficulties with biometric fingerprint authentication on their identity cards. They can complete the registration process using an OTP sent to their linked mobile number.MSRTC has urged all eligible senior citizens and women passengers to complete their NCMC registration before October 1 to ensure uninterrupted, transparent and hassle-free travel.
Article Summary: The National Common Mobility Card (NCMC) will be mandatory for senior citizens, Amrit senior citizens and women passengers. The move aims to streamline and digitise travel concessions on state transport buses. Card registration and distribution have already begun at bus stations and depots across Maharashtra.

Article Title: Seoul built an architectural installation from mushrooms and agricultural waste; its walls were grown rather than constructed
Article Text:
Walls of Public Life. Image Credit: ANOMALIA

Seoul’s mycelium walls turn mushroom waste into architecture

Image Credit: ANOMALIA

The wall was grown through a low-energy process

What made the facade different from an ordinary wall

The project connected Mumbai, Bandung and Seoul

What could grown building materials offer future architecture

Seoul became the setting for an unique architectural experiment in 2025, where a public installation was made from mushroom mycelium and agricultural waste instead of conventional building materials. Named as Walls of Public Life, the project was created by Mumbai-based Anomalia for the 5th Seoul Biennale of Architecture and Urbanism. Its blocks were grown using fungal networks that bind crop waste together, turning discarded organic material into lightweight building components. The installation offered a different way of thinking about walls, showing how some future construction materials could be cultivated rather than manufactured.The Walls of Public Life installation was created for the first outdoor exhibition of the Seoul Biennale, held at Songhyeon Green Plaza. According to Anomalia’s project website, the studio was invited to create one of 24 Walls of Public Life for the 2025 event, curated by Thomas Heatherwick. The project explored what building facades could become if they were grown from mushroom mycelium rather than produced entirely through conventional industrial processes.The material at the centre of the installation was mycelium, the root-like network of fungi. Instead of treating agricultural waste as something to discard, the project used it as the main growing material. Crop waste was mixed with mycelium cultures, allowing the fungal network to spread through the organic material and naturally hold it together.This gave the waste a new purpose. Anomalia states that each block used 2.1 kilograms of crop waste while weighing about 1.5 kilograms. The resulting material could then be shaped into architectural components without relying on the energy-intensive processes normally associated with many conventional construction materials.The production method was relatively straightforward. Once the crop waste and mycelium cultures were combined, the mixture was placed into moulds. The fungal network grew through the material and acted as a natural binding system. The blocks were then dried and stabilised, producing the components used for the Seoul installation.Architecture Lab, in its report on Walls of Public Life, describes the installation as being made from MycoBlox and Biobo panels, which are mycelium-based materials combined with agricultural byproducts. The fungal networks bind the organic material as they grow, producing lightweight components with significant compressive strength.Anomalia’s own account gives the blocks a tested compressive capacity of up to 1.5 tons. That detail is important because the project was not simply about making an unusual surface from mushrooms. It was also an attempt to demonstrate that materials grown from biological processes could have practical qualities suitable for architectural use.The installation was designed to look and behave differently from the sealed surfaces commonly found on buildings. Its porous structure allowed air and light to pass through, while its uneven texture created a surface that could be experienced through touch as well as sight. MYCL , the Indonesian material company involved in the research and production, describes the installation as a breathable and interactive facade. Its account says the MycoBlox provided 3D modular blocks, while the square BIBO panels created another layer within the structure.Instead of functioning simply as a solid division between people and their surroundings, the installation was intended to create a more open relationship between the structure, visitors and the surrounding environment.The unique wall was also the result of work spread across three countries. According to Anomalia, the design was developed in Mumbai, India, while the materials were grown in Bandung, Indonesia, in collaboration with MYCL. The finished components were then transported to South Korea and assembled at Songhyeon Green Plaza in Seoul.MYCL similarly describes the project as a cross-border collaboration between architectural design and material research. Its production model avoided the idea that every part of a building material has to come from a conventional high-heat manufacturing facility.The collaboration also brought together different areas of expertise. Anomalia handled design and research, while MYCL worked on material research and production. The project was supported by the Seoul Metropolitan Government and P4G(Partnering for Green Growth and the Global Goals 2030).The Seoul installation presented mycelium materials as biodegradable and carbon negative. MYCL describes that the materials were designed to return to the earth at the end of their useful life.Another feature was the use of a modular wooden framework. MYCL notes that the framework allowed the installation to be disassembled, supporting a more circular approach to construction rather than treating the structure as something permanently fixed in place. Architecture Lab describes Walls of Public Life as a practical test of mycelium composite blocks in an outdoor public setting, where the material faced rain, storms, humidity and regular human interaction.
Article Summary: Walls of Public Life was created by Mumbai-based Anomalia for the 5th Seoul Biennale of Architecture and Urbanism. Its blocks were grown using fungal networks that bind crop waste together, turning discarded organic material into lightweight building components. The installation was designed to look and behave differently from the sealed surfaces commonly found on buildings.

Article Title: Meet Erin Gardner, the Westford student raising $2,200 to rebuild a 24-foot trail bridge; she has already raised $1,125 and plans to replace its railings so children can safely keep using the path
Article Text:
A bridge that has connected the community for years

The project is also an Eagle Scout milestone

Her connection to the outdoors

A project backed by local support

A deteriorating trail bridge in Westford, Massachusetts, is at the centre of a student-led effort to preserve an important route used by children and families in the community. Westford Academy student Erin Gardner is raising $2,200 to restore a damaged section of the bridge as part of her Eagle Scout project, according to a September 24 report by The Westford Villager, published through WestfordCAT. Details on Gardner’s fundraising page confirm that the planned work includes rebuilding a 24-foot portion of the structure and replacing its railings.The bridge, known locally as the Academy Bridge, forms part of a network of wooded trails connecting Westford Academy with nearby schools and recreational areas. For years, the trails have offered students a way to move between the schools and surrounding sports fields without relying entirely on roads.Time, however, has taken a toll on the wooden structure. A 24-foot section has deteriorated to the point where part of it has fallen toward the water below, while the railings also require replacement.Rather than allowing the crossing to become unusable, Gardner has taken on the task of helping restore it. Her GoFundMe campaign sets a $2,200 fundraising target, with the money intended to support the materials and work required for the restoration.When The Westford Villager reported on the project on September 24, the campaign had collected $1,125.For Gardner, the bridge is not simply a community repair project. It is also part of her journey toward earning the rank of Eagle Scout, one of the highest achievements available in Scouting.The project gives her an opportunity to put the leadership and service skills she has developed through Scouting into practice while addressing something that has a direct impact on people around her. According to her fundraising page, the restoration will focus on replacing the damaged 24-foot portion and installing new railings along the bridge. Once completed, the work is expected to make the crossing usable for the community again.Gardner’s choice of project also reflects her wider involvement in outdoor activities. She is a member of Westford Academy’s Cirrus club, an organisation that encourages students to spend time outdoors and build connections through activities in nature.The group has organised hikes and overnight outdoor challenges, including trips to places such as Mount Monadnock. For students involved, these activities offer a break from the routines of school and an opportunity to spend time outdoors with friends.Gardner has previously spoken about the appeal of simply being outside, whether through hiking, climbing or informal activities with other students. That connection makes the bridge project particularly fitting. The structure is part of the same network of trails that allows students to experience the wooded landscape around their schools.Gardner’s Scouting journey has also earned recognition from people in the Westford community. Local resident Barbara Evangelista highlighted Gardner’s years of involvement in Scouts, including leadership responsibilities and participation in a 12-day Philmont trek, in a Facebook post referenced by The Westford Villager.The restoration campaign now brings those years of service into a project with a visible community purpose. Instead of creating something entirely new, Gardner is working to preserve a route that local students have already relied on for years.If the fundraising goal is reached, the damaged section and railings can be replaced, allowing the Academy Bridge to continue serving as a connection between the surrounding schools, trails and sports areas. For Gardner, reaching that goal would mean more than completing an Eagle Scout requirement. It would mean leaving behind a practical improvement that other children in Westford can continue to use long after her own school years are over.
Article Summary: Westford Academy student Erin Gardner is raising $2,200 to restore a damaged section of the bridge as part of her Eagle Scout project. The bridge, known locally as the Academy Bridge, forms part of a network of wooded trails connecting Westford Academy with nearby schools and recreational areas. A 24-foot section has deteriorated to the point where part of it has fallen toward the water below.

Article Title: In 2002, Scotland opened the Falkirk Wheel to lift boats 100 feet between canals, replacing 11 locks with a rotating 1,800-tonne structure
Article Text:
PC: Wikipedia

How the Falkirk Wheel replaced 11 locks with a rotating boat lift

How the Falkirk Wheel raises boats 100 feet between two Scottish canals

PC: Wikipedia

How the Falkirk Wheel uses 1.5 kWh to rotate its 1,800-tonne structure

How the Falkirk Wheel cut a full-day canal journey to just a few minutes

Opened in 2002, the Falkirk Wheel transformed how boats travel between two historic canals in central Scotland. The rotating boat lift connects the Forth and Clyde Canal with the Union Canal, which lies about 100 feet higher. Instead of relying on the former flight of 11 locks, the structure uses two water-filled gondolas that rotate to raise and lower vessels. The system was designed to keep the gondolas balanced, allowing the 1,800-tonne structure to operate using just 1.5 kWh for each rotation, according to Scottish Canals. The energy used is commonly compared with that required to boil eight kettles.The Falkirk Wheel was built as part of efforts to restore the Forth and Clyde Canal and the Union Canal. The Forth and Clyde Canal was built in 1790, while the Union Canal opened in 1822. The two waterways had originally been connected at Falkirk through a series of 11 locks, but the locks later became unusable, and the canals were eventually closed.The restoration project sought a new way to connect the waterways rather than simply rebuilding the old staircase of locks. The Linda Hall Library says British Waterways Scotland worked with architectural and engineering firms to develop a unique boat-lift design.The resulting structure uses two gondolas positioned on opposite sides of the rotating wheel, allowing boats to be raised and lowered as the wheel turns.Each side of the Falkirk Wheel contains a gondola capable of carrying canal boats. The Linda Hall Library states that each gondola can accommodate up to four canal boats, or one or two larger boats. Once the boats enter, seals are raised to make the gondolas watertight, and the wheel rotates to exchange their positions. Scottish Canals similarly describes the Wheel as connecting the two canals 35 metres above.A central feature of the design is the balance between the two gondolas. The two gondolas, when full of water, weigh the same regardless of how many boats they contain. It attributes this to Archimedes’ principle: when a boat enters a full gondola, it displaces water equal to its own weight, leaving the total weight unchanged.According to Scottish Canals, the structure weighs 1,800 tonnes and uses just 1.5 kWh for each rotation. The Linda Hall Library gives a figure of about 1.5 kilowatt-hours for one half-turn and notes the commonly cited comparison that this is about the same amount of energy required to boil eight kettles of water.Before the Wheel was built, vessels travelling between the two canals had to pass through the former flight of 11 locks. Scottish Canals says this meant opening and closing 44 lock gates and could take a full day. The Wheel reduced the canal transfer to a journey of only a few minutes.Since opening, the Falkirk Wheel has also become a major visitor destination. Scottish Canals says it attracts around 500,000 visitors each year and describes it as one of Scotland's busiest tourist attractions. The organisation calls it a "working sculpture" combining modern engineering and technology with principles associated with Archimedes.
Article Summary: The Falkirk Wheel was built as part of efforts to restore the Forth and Clyde Canal and the Union Canal. The structure uses two water-filled gondolas that rotate to raise and lower vessels. The 1,800-tonne structure uses just 1.5 kWh for each rotation, according to Scottish Canals.

Article Title: London designer turns waste mussel shells and local Thames sand into glass; wins £10,000 Design Museum prize
Article Text:
Representative Image of a designer creating glass objects using quagga mussel shells and local materials from the River Thames (AI Generated Image)

Quagga mussel shells became one of the key ingredients

Thames Glass grew from a collaboration with Thames Water

The material has also been tested as architectural cladding

The prize will support Harrison's next stage of research

London designer Lulu Harrison has won the 2025 Ralph Saltzman Prize from the Design Museum for Thames Glass, a project that turns locally sourced and waste materials into glass. Harrison's recipes use materials including sand from around the River Thames, wood ash and waste quagga mussel shells supplied by Thames Water. The Design Museum describes Harrison as a geo-alchemist glass artist whose project explores the possibility of creating geo-specific glass from abundant and waste materials associated with a particular place. Harrison was selected as the fourth recipient of the annual prize by a jury comprising industrial designer Konstantin Grcic, material designer Seetal Solanki, artist and designer Stephen Burks and design journalist and author Michelle Ogundehin, alongside Lisa Saltzman. The judges praised Harrison's research and her approach to mapping the raw materials used in the glass and communicating that process to audiences. She received a £10,000 bursary to continue developing her work. This innovative project demonstrates how creative material science can transform environmental waste streams into artistic and functional applications, offering promising possibilities for sustainable design innovation.A central component of Thames Glass is the shell of the quagga mussel, an invasive non-native species that can cause blockages in Thames Water's transfer tunnels and has to be removed. Harrison says her collaboration with Thames Water gave her access to the waste shells, which would otherwise require disposal. She combines ground-up mussel shells with local sand and waste wood ash to create different glass recipes. Her own project description says the work began with experiments using local and waste materials sourced in and around the Thames, including waste shells from water companies and wood ash or bracken from surrounding forests. The resulting glass has been used to create objects including carafes, tumblers and other vessels, with the material's natural impurities contributing to its distinctive appearance. Harrison developed the project while studying for an MA in Material Futures at Central Saint Martins and has worked with glassblowers, glass chemists and glass archaeologists during its development.The project developed through Harrison's work with Thames Water while she was studying at Central Saint Martins. Harrison has said that the collaboration helped her find a use for the tonnes of quagga mussel shells being removed because the animals were blocking water infrastructure. Her early work produced prototypes of a Thames Glass carafe and tumbler, while later experiments explored other forms and applications. Central Saint Martins documented the project in 2022, describing Harrison's use of local sands, waste shells and wood ash and her collaboration with Thames Water. Harrison has also worked with Here Design, glassblowers and other specialists to develop the material and its applications. Rather than presenting Thames Glass as a replacement for conventional glass, Harrison describes the project as an exploration of alternative glassmaking recipes based on materials associated with a particular geographical area.Harrison later worked with London architecture studio Bureau de Change to investigate whether Thames Glass could be used on buildings. The collaboration produced a series of cast glass façade tiles made using the material, with patterns inspired by London's architectural history, including designs found on 19th-century terracotta chimney pots. The tiles were presented as part of Beautility: How Fusing Beauty and Function Can Change the World, an exhibition curated by Here Design during London Craft Week. Bureau de Change says the project explored whether Thames Glass could be used as an alternative material for building cladding, while Harrison's own project page describes the tiles as an exploration of future applications for the material. The collaboration therefore moved Thames Glass beyond vessels and into architectural experimentation, although the work remains a design and material research project rather than an established commercial building product.The Ralph Saltzman Prize gives Harrison £10,000 to continue developing Thames Glass and provides an opportunity to display the project at the Design Museum. The museum describes the prize as an annual award for emerging product designers whose practices explore new directions in design, including technical innovation, sustainability and cultural re-evaluation. Harrison's 2025 project was displayed at the museum from June 24 to August 25, 2025. In describing the award, Harrison said her practice is driven by research, process, collaboration, experimentation and hands-on making, connecting craft and science while exploring more localised possibilities for glassmaking. Thames Glass is still fundamentally an experimental material project, but its use of waste quagga mussel shells, local sand and waste ash demonstrates how materials removed from one system can become ingredients in another.
Article Summary: London designer Lulu Harrison has won the 2025 Ralph Saltzman Prize for Thames Glass. The project uses locally sourced and waste materials to create glass. Harrison's recipes use materials including sand from around the River Thames, wood ash and waste quagga mussel shells supplied by Thames Water. The prize will support Harrison's next stage of research.

Article Title: Bentley launches first fully electric Torcal in 107-year history at £173,000, undercutting Ferrari Luce with 375-mile range and 10-80% charging in under 20 minutes
Article Text:
Bentley has launched the Torcal, its first fully electric vehicle in 107 years. (Photo: Bentley)

Bentley says wealthy buyers are increasingly accepting EVs

Torcal specifications in detail

The Bentley Torcal offers a driving range of up to 375 miles. (Photo: Bentley)

New Bentley design language debuts with the Torcal

Bentley has combined electric performance with its signature luxury design and handcrafted cabin. (Photo: Bentley)

Cabin combines leather, wood, wool and aluminium with digital technology

The Bentley Torcal starts at £173,000, significantly below Ferrari’s Luce EV. (Photo: Bentley)

Four Experience modes change the character of the car

Bentley recreates engine character for its electric SUV

S version brings a more aggressive exterior

Bentley wants the Torcal to remain a Bentley first

British luxury carmaker Bentley Motors has entered the electric vehicle market with the launch of the all-new Torcal, its first fully electric model in the company’s 107-year history. The new electric SUV marks a significant step for Bentley as the luxury automotive industry continues to test the appetite of affluent buyers for high-performance EVs.The Torcal, which was unveiled in London on Wednesday evening, becomes the fourth model in Bentley’s current line-up alongside the Continental GT, Flying Spur and Bentayga. Designed and engineered at Bentley’s headquarters in Crewe, northwest England, the electric SUV has been developed to combine the brand’s traditional craftsmanship with new electric technology, performance and a completely new design language.The Torcal starts at £173,000, or around $229,000, placing it substantially below Ferrari’s first electric vehicle, the Luce, which carries a reported starting price of around €550,000 ($626,000). Ferrari launched the Luce three months before Bentley’s EV, with its design drawing mixed reactions from some observers and analysts.Speaking to CNBC’s Squawk Box Europe, Bentley Motors chairman and CEO Frank-Steffen Walliser said the Torcal sits at the entry level of Bentley’s price range and has received positive reactions across markets.Walliser said Bentley was not looking at Ferrari’s Luce launch for lessons because the development of a luxury vehicle is a long-term process. He pointed out that Bentley works on a roughly four-year development cycle and cannot change direction simply in response to what another manufacturer has launched.According to Walliser, acceptance of electric cars among Bentley’s wealthy clientele is continuing to grow, with customers becoming increasingly knowledgeable about EV technology.The comments come as several luxury manufacturers reassess their electric strategies. Porsche and Lamborghini, for instance, have scaled back aspects of their EV plans amid weaker-than-expected demand in parts of the luxury electric-car market.Bentley’s approach with the Torcal has been to make the vehicle feel like a Bentley first, regardless of its powertrain. The company says particular attention has been paid to design, driving behaviour, sound and the overall sensory experience.The Torcal is a five-metre-long electric SUV and is the shortest four-door Bentley yet produced. It has a wheelbase designed to maximise cabin space while its short overhangs, long bonnet and upright front end give it the powerful stance Bentley wanted for its new design direction.The electric SUV offers a driving range of up to 375 miles, or approximately 600 km, depending on specification and conditions. Bentley says the vehicle can charge from 10% to 80% in less than 20 minutes when connected to a 400kW charging system. The company also says around 100 miles of range can be added in seven minutes.Two versions will be available at launch: the Core and the S.The Core version develops 810bhp and 1,194Nm of torque. It can accelerate from 0 to 60mph in 3.3 seconds and has a top speed of 155mph.The more performance-focused S produces 876bhp and up to 1,350Nm of torque with Launch Control. It can accelerate from 0 to 60mph in just 2.8 seconds, while its top speed rises to 162mph.Bentley says the electric powertrain allows the Torcal to combine supercar-like acceleration with what it describes as year-round usability.The vehicle provides 460 litres of boot space, while a further 90-litre front luggage compartment is available under the bonnet. Its turning circle is 11.1 metres, an important consideration for a vehicle measuring around five metres in length.The Torcal represents the production interpretation of Bentley’s EXP 15 concept, which was first revealed in 2025. Its design introduces a new visual direction for the marque while retaining elements intended to connect the electric SUV with Bentley’s heritage.Lead designer Robin Page describes the design process through four key areas: proportion, graphical elements, surface language and detail.The long wheelbase, short overhangs, long bonnet and upright front create what Bentley calls a “powerful stance” and “upright elegance”. The company says the proportions are intended to make the Torcal immediately recognisable as a Bentley despite its new electric architecture.The front features an illuminated diamond grille and advanced lighting elements. The rear graphics form what Bentley describes as a prestigious shield, while several design cues reference the EXP 15 concept and historic Bentley models, including the Continental T.Rather than relying on numerous character lines, Bentley has used a more sculptural approach. The surfaces taper towards the rear, creating what the company describes as the appearance of a “resting beast”.The diamond pattern seen on the exterior continues into the cabin, creating a visual link between the outside and inside of the vehicle.Inside, the Torcal blends traditional Bentley materials with modern technology.The dashboard takes inspiration from a wing and combines leather, wood or veneer and aluminium. Bentley has retained physical controls in key areas, including the centre console and steering wheel, while curved OLED displays provide the main digital interface.The seats offer 16-way adjustment, along with heating, ventilation, adjustable bolsters and massage functions. Optional postural adjustment and smart climate functions are also available.A wellness-focused seat function can provide leg massage, adding another element to Bentley’s emphasis on long-distance comfort.The company has also placed considerable emphasis on sustainable material choices. The cabin can use leather, wood, wool and aluminium, including what Bentley describes as the world’s first 100% Merino wool automotive fabric, which is certified by the Responsible Wool Standard.Sustainably sourced walnut offcuts are also used in the interior.For additional practicality, Bentley has introduced power-folding rear seats for the first time in the model.The Torcal features four Experience modes that alter various aspects of the vehicle, including lighting, sound, climate, airflow and the amount of digital information presented to the driver.Comfort mode is designed around a calmer environment and a more relaxed experience, including what Bentley describes as a digital detox approach.Sport mode, meanwhile, increases the intensity of the experience with a more immersive soundtrack and changes to the lighting and other cabin elements.Facial-recognition technology can also identify individual occupants and automatically adjust settings such as the seat, steering wheel and certain advanced driver-assistance system preferences.The Torcal uses a network of 25 radars, sensors and cameras to support its driver-assistance and vehicle-monitoring systems.One of the more distinctive aspects of the Torcal is its approach to sound.Instead of leaving the cabin silent, Bentley has created the Bentley Dynamic Symphony, an artificial soundtrack designed around the rhythms and character associated with the company’s historic combustion engines.The sound incorporates elements inspired by Bentley’s 6¾-litre V8, combined with drums, viola and bass guitar.The soundtrack is calibrated to the vehicle’s torque demand and speed, with the intensity, volume and feedback increasing when the driver selects Sport mode.Bentley has also developed a more advanced audio system for the cabin. The standard system produces 620 watts through 16 speakers, while the optional system delivers 1,780 watts through 28 speakers with Dolby Atmos. The upgraded system also incorporates kinaesthetic seat shakers and speakers positioned in the front headrests.The Torcal S receives additional styling changes to distinguish it from the Core version.These include black exterior brightware, black mirror caps, darker rear lamps, rear diffusers and sportier side sills. The front bumper also receives additional strakes, while red brake calipers add another performance-oriented visual element.Inside, the S introduces its own colour split, quilting and stitching treatments.While the S offers the highest output at 876bhp, Bentley says the focus is not simply on outright acceleration. The company has attempted to combine the additional performance with the comfort, refinement and usability traditionally associated with its luxury grand tourers and SUVs.The Torcal arrives at a critical point for the luxury EV market, where manufacturers are balancing increasingly powerful electric drivetrains with changing customer expectations.Bentley’s first fully electric model was originally expected to arrive earlier, but its launch was pushed back amid softer demand for luxury electric vehicles.The company is now betting that its established design language, handcrafted interior, high performance and focus on sound and sensory experience can make the transition to electric power feel familiar to existing Bentley customers.With a starting price of £173,000, a range of up to 375 miles, charging from 10% to 80% in less than 20 minutes and as much as 876bhp in S specification, the Torcal represents Bentley’s attempt to bring electric propulsion into its traditional luxury performance formula.The model is expected to go on sale by the end of the year, although the extensive range of available options can push the final price significantly higher.
Article Summary: Bentley Torcal is first fully electric model in the company's 107-year history. It starts at £173,000, significantly below Ferrari’s Luce EV. The Torcal offers a driving range of up to 375 miles and can accelerate from 0 to 60mph in 3.3 seconds.

Article Title: A retired UK rail engineer turned his East Sussex garden into a working railway using a Victorian platelayer’s trolley; the line now runs 50 feet and uses a 12-volt battery charged by solar power
Article Text:
During the Covid-19 lockdown in 2020, Backshall began developing a railway in the garden of his home in Willingdon, East Sussex (Image Credit: George Carden/BBC)

From railway career to garden railway

A 50-foot railway in the garden

Backshall's garden contains a collection of authentic railway-related objects, including signs, signals and other equipment (Image Credit: George Carden/BBC)

From hand power to solar energy

Railway memorabilia fills the garden

A lockdown project that kept growing

A former railway engineer has transformed his garden in East Sussex into an unusual working railway, complete with full-size track, a vintage-style carriage and railway memorabilia. Railway Magazine, which featured Adrian Backshall’s project, describes the 50-foot line as a Wickham lookalike built on an old platelayer’s trolley. The small railway now uses a 12-volt car battery charged by a solar panel to power its winch, allowing the carriage to travel slowly along the garden track. What began as a lockdown project has since grown into a distinctive railway-themed garden attraction for Backshall, his family and guests.Adrian Backshall retired from Network Rail in 2018 after a career working on Britain's railways. His connection with railway equipment, however, did not end with retirement. During the Covid-19 lockdown in 2020, Backshall began developing a railway in the garden of his home in Willingdon, East Sussex. The project gave him a way to put his railway knowledge and collection of equipment to use while spending more time at home.The centrepiece is a carriage based on a Victorian platelayer's trolley. A friend who was a blacksmith helped create the Wickham-style body that sits on top of the original trolley.Platelayers' trolleys were lightweight railway vehicles historically used by railway workers to travel along tracks while carrying tools and equipment. Backshall's version retains the character of such a vehicle while giving it a new purpose as a garden railway carriage.What started as a much shorter line has now become a 50-foot railway running through the garden. Some of the track used in the project dates back to 1898, giving the otherwise modern garden installation a genuine connection with railway history. Backshall has also added railway signs, signals and other pieces of equipment around the property, making the garden resemble a miniature railway museum.The railway has two main stopping points, near the garden shed and patio. The line is not designed for speed. Instead, the carriage moves slowly enough for passengers to enjoy the unusual surroundings as it makes its journey through the garden. According to Railway Magazine, the 50-foot cable-worked railway has a maximum speed of about 0.3 miles per hour. That extremely slow pace is part of the charm of the project. Rather than trying to recreate a conventional railway journey, Backshall has created something closer to a moving garden room with a genuine railway feel.The railway has also evolved technically since its early days. Initially, the carriage was moved using a hand-cranked pulley arrangement. As the project expanded, Backshall replaced that system with a 12-volt winch. The winch is powered by a 12-volt car battery, which is charged using a solar panel. This allows the railway to operate without relying on a conventional mains-powered system for its movement.The arrangement combines old railway equipment with simple modern technology. A Victorian-era trolley forms the basis of the carriage, while solar power provides the energy needed to move it along the track. The result is a small but functioning railway that reflects Backshall's interest in both railway history and engineering.The track is only part of the transformation. Backshall's garden contains a collection of authentic railway-related objects, including signs, signals and other equipment. Some of the signs retain the language associated with working railway lines, giving visitors the impression that they have stepped into a small railway installation rather than an ordinary residential garden.Inside the carriage, the railway theme continues. The cabin has seating for four people and includes a wood-burning stove, while railway memorabilia and other details make the space suitable for entertaining. Backshall and his wife Ruth have used the train for gatherings and tea parties, turning the unusual railway into part of their home life. The project has also involved some negotiation over space. As the railway was extended, the track passed through part of the garden that had previously been used for flowers. Ruth has spoken about the changes with humour, while supporting the project that began as a lockdown idea.Backshall's railway demonstrates how a small hobby can develop into a much more elaborate personal project. The original lockdown railway was considerably shorter, but the line has since been extended to 50 feet. The addition of a solar-powered winch has also made the operation more convenient than the original hand-powered arrangement. For someone who spent decades around Britain's railways, the project offers a way to preserve that connection after retirement. Instead of simply displaying an old trolley, Backshall has incorporated it into a functioning railway environment. The garden railway has also attracted wider attention. Backshall and Ruth held an open day in June 2025 to raise money for St Wilfrid's Hospice, allowing the unusual project to serve a charitable purpose as well.Today, the 50-foot line stands as an unusual combination of railway history, engineering and gardening. With its Victorian trolley, historic track, railway signs and solar-powered 12-volt system, Backshall's creation has turned an ordinary East Sussex garden into a working piece of railway heritage.
Article Summary: Adrian Backshall retired from Network Rail in 2018 after a career working on Britain's railways. During the Covid-19 lockdown in 2020, Backshall began developing a railway in the garden of his home in Willingdon, East Sussex. The railway now uses a 12-volt car battery charged by a solar panel to power its winch, allowing the carriage to travel slowly along the track.

Article Title: OpenAI agents scanned UN data hub over 16,000 times, used aggressive access methods: Report
Article Text:
OpenAI agents repeatedly accessed UN data hub

OpenAI agents flooded a United Nations website with search requests and employed multiple aggressive methods to access data from the system in June, an independent research report published Saturday found, according to The Wall Street Journal.Researchers have identified several instances in recent weeks in which OpenAI’s artificial-intelligence models exhibited unexpected behaviour online. In the UN case, as with several other incidents reported in recent days, the agents used extensive methods to retrieve data from websites.The agents scanned a publicly available online data hub operated by UN Trade and Development, the organisation’s trade arm, more than 16,000 times between April and the end of June. According to Howard-Jones, the bots appeared to have been tasked with retrieving publicly available information but resorted to extreme methods when they encountered obstacles.In one instance, the agents bypassed a filter blocking their data requests and ultimately used a technique that the website operators did not permit, she found. Howard-Jones, an engineer, has spent recent weeks tracking public evidence of OpenAI agents’ online activity.OpenAI said on Friday that it is conducting a broad, ongoing review “of misaligned models during training and evaluation” and studying “a high volume of actions” they have taken.“We’re reviewing these findings and have reached out to the UN to offer a briefing with the team conducting that review,” an OpenAI spokeswoman said.OpenAI said most of the activity it has reviewed so far involved “routine research tasks, such as accessing public web content to answer questions,” but added, “we realize anyone impacted takes this seriously and we do too.” The spokeswoman said its models use government websites as authoritative sources of public information.Leaders of major AI companies have recently called for a coordinated slowdown in model development before the technology advances to a point where humans could lose control. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman has also suggested that the company may need to delay its IPO to focus on safety.The development comes after OpenAI disclosed on Friday that its artificial-intelligence agents had interacted with several US government websites in unexpected ways. The company said its models accessed publicly available information on two websites operated by the Securities and Exchange Commission, as well as data from the US Census Bureau.OpenAI said it found no use of SEC credentials, access to accounts or nonpublic information, changes to SEC data or systems, or evidence of a compromise or vulnerability.
Article Summary: OpenAI agents flooded a UN website with search requests and employed multiple aggressive methods to access data from the system in June. Researchers have identified several instances in recent weeks in which OpenAI’s artificial- intelligence models exhibited unexpected behaviour online. The development comes after OpenAI disclosed on Friday that its models had interacted with several US government websites in unexpected ways.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:
AI image

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.

How Jeevan Pramaan simplifies pensioner verification



Every year, lakhs of pensioners across India must prove that they are still alive to continue receiving their pension. This verification, known as the Life Certificate or Digital Life Certificate (DLC), is a crucial and mandatory step in ensuring that pension payments are made only to eligible recipients, preventing fraud and misuse.Traditionally, this process involved visiting the bank or pension office in person, standing in long queues, and submitting a signed paper certificate. However, with the government’s focus on digitisation and technological advancement, this process has become much simpler, faster, and more convenient. Pensioners can now submit their certificates digitally from the comfort of their homes using Jeevan Pramaan, a secure, user-friendly, and Aadhaar-based platform.A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries.The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric-enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.Introduced by the Government of India, it uses Aadhaar-based biometric authentication using either fingerprint or iris scan to verify a pensioner’s identity. Once verified, a digital certificate is automatically generated and shared with authorised pension disbursing agencies.This online process eliminates the need for physical verification, providing elderly pensioners with a simpler and more accessible way to maintain their pension benefits.According to PIB, The submission of the Life Certificate is mandatory for all pensioners who wish to continue receiving their pension without interruption. For the year 2025, the standard submission period is betweenTo make the process more comfortable for the elderly, the government allows pensioners aged 80 years and above to begin the submission process earlier, from 1 October 2025. This extended window gives senior citizens more time and flexibility to complete the procedure without facing last-minute difficulties.The Jeevan Pramaan process involves two main steps: registering the biometric device and generating the digital certificate.Before using the service, pensioners or operators must register their biometric device such as a fingerprint or iris scanner. During registration, the user provides their Aadhaar number and mobile number, after which an OTP (One-Time Password) is sent to their mobile. After entering the OTP, they must provide their name and email ID before scanning their fingerprint or iris.Once authentication is complete, the system confirms that device registration was successful, allowing the user to move to the next step.In this step, the pensioner enters personal details such as Aadhaar number, mobile number, name, PPO number, pension type, sanctioning authority, disbursing agency, and bank account details. The system also asks whether the pensioner has remarried or is re-employed.After entering all details, the pensioner scans their fingerprint or iris using the registered biometric device. Upon successful authentication, the Digital Life Certificate is generated, and an SMS acknowledgment with the Jeevan Pramaan Certificate ID is sent to the registered mobile number.This certificate is automatically stored in the Life Certificate Repository, accessible anytime to both pensioners and pension agencies.Once the Digital Life Certificate is created, it can be electronically delivered to the concerned Pension Disbursing Agency (PDA). PDAs can log in to the Jeevan Pramaan portal to view, verify, or download the certificate directly.Pensioners can also download a PDF copy of their certificate by visiting the Jeevan Pramaan website and entering their Pramaan ID or Aadhaar number. This ensures transparency and easy access for future reference.The government provides several options to submit the Life Certificate, allowing pensioners to choose the method that suits them best.Pensioners who prefer traditional methods can visit their bank branch or a Citizen Service Centre (CSC) to submit their Life Certificate physically. Trained staff at these centres assist pensioners in verifying their details and completing the process.For those unable to travel due to age or health issues, India Post Payments Bank (IPPB) offers a doorstep banking service. Pensioners can schedule an appointment, and an IPPB representative will visit their home to complete the submission using biometric authentication. This service is available for both IPPB and non-IPPB account holders.For pensioners comfortable with technology, the Jeevan Pramaan portal provides a completely online process. By visiting https://jeevanpramaan.gov.in, pensioners can submit their Digital Life Certificate using a computer, laptop, or smartphone equipped with a fingerprint or iris scanner.The system uses the Aadhaar platform to authenticate biometric details. Once verification is successful, a Digital Life Certificate is generated and stored in a secure online repository. Pension disbursing agencies can then directly access the certificate, removing the need for physical paperwork.The UMANG (Unified Mobile Application for New-age Governance) app offers another easy option. Pensioners can download the app from the Google Play Store, search for “Jeevan Pramaan,” and select “Generate Life Certificate.”After entering the necessary details such as Aadhaar number, PPO number, and type of pension, pensioners must authenticate themselves using biometric verification. The app then generates a Digital Life Certificate (DLC), which is automatically shared with the pension disbursing authority.All pensioners who receive government, defence, or private sector pensions through authorised disbursing agencies are required to submit their Life Certificate every year. This includes:Failure to submit the certificate within the stipulated period may result in temporary suspension of pension payments until verification is completed.To ensure a smooth submission process, pensioners should keep certain details and documents ready. These include:Having these details ready helps to avoid delays or errors during authentication, whether submitting online or offline.Yes, an Aadhaar number or Virtual ID (VID) is mandatory to generate a Digital Life Certificate. The entire Jeevan Pramaan system is based on Aadhaar authentication, which ensures accuracy and prevents fraud. Pensioners must make sure their Aadhaar is linked with their mobile number and bank account before attempting to generate the certificate.The Digital Life Certificate is fully valid and legally recognised under the Information Technology Act. Pension disbursing authorities across India accept it as an official document, equivalent to the traditional paper-based life certificate.Its biometric verification system makes it secure and tamper-proof, reducing the chances of wrongful pension disbursal or misuse of pension funds.Before the introduction of Jeevan Pramaan, pensioners often faced difficulties in submitting their certificates, especially those with health problems or limited mobility. The digital system has removed these challenges, allowing pensioners to submit their verification anytime and anywhere.By integrating biometric technology and Aadhaar authentication, Jeevan Pramaan has streamlined pension management, improving efficiency for both pensioners and government departments. It also enhances transparency and ensures that genuine beneficiaries receive payments on time.
Article Summary: A Life Certificate is an official document that confirms a pensioner is alive. Without it, pension payments are automatically paused by the pension disbursing agency. This verification is essential for preventing fraudulent claims and ensuring that pensions reach the rightful beneficiaries. The Digital Life Certificate (DLC), also known as Jeevan Pramaan, is an advanced biometric- enabled version of the traditional paper certificate.

Article Title: How to get your CIBIL credit score without a PAN card
Article Text:

What is a CIBIL score?

How to get your CIBIL Credit score without a PAN Card

Factors affecting your CIBIL score

CIBIL credit score : Understanding your creditworthiness is pivotal in today's financial landscape, especially when seeking loans or credit cards. The Credit Information Bureau (India) Limited, commonly known as CIBIL, plays an important role in this regard by providing credit scores to borrowers.According to ET, credit score helps banks make informed decisions about extending credit cards and loans. Your credit history influences your CIBIL score , which is calculated using a special method.Your CIBIL score is a three-digit number that reflects your creditworthiness and repayment capacity. Ranging from 300 to 900, a higher score indicates a stronger likelihood of loan approval. Banks and financial institutions use this score to assess the risk associated with lending money.1. Go to the official CIBIL website and click on 'Personal CIBIL score,' then 'Get Your Free CIBIL score.' Follow the link provided and fill in all the required details.2. If you don’t have a PAN Card, you can use an alternative identification such as Passport, Voter ID, Driver’s License, or Ration Card. Enter the number of the chosen ID.3. Provide your date of birth, PIN code, and select your state. Finally, enter your mobile number and click on ‘Accept and Continue’.4. Authenticate your identity by entering the OTP (One-Time Password) delivered to your mobile device on the next screen. Click 'Continue' to proceed.5. Choose whether you want to link the device with your account. Select 'Yes' or 'No' based on your preference.6. Upon successful registration, you will see a page confirming that 'You have successfully registered!'7. Click on ‘Go to Dashboard’ to access and view your CIBIL score.The factors influencing the new CIBIL score, as stated on the CIBIL website, include:1. Depth of credit: This refers to the duration of your existing credit history, calculated from the opening date of your oldest credit account.2. Long-term trend of outstanding balances: The overall trend of outstanding balances over time affects your score.3. Transaction history on credit cards: How you manage transactions on your credit cards impacts your score.4. Ratio of actual repayment amount to total amount due: This ratio indicates your repayment behavior and influences your score accordingly.5. Number of new accounts opened and number of accounts closed: Opening or closing accounts can affect your score, so managing these actions wisely is important.
